summary:
Diane Lin, Tech Lead at Datadog, presents on agent inconsistency—the phenomenon where the same model given the same input produces semantically different outputs across runs. While many dismiss this as LLM stochasticity, Lin argues it is a critical product flaw that destroys customer trust, particularly in high-stakes domains like cybersecurity where a verdict flipping between malicious and benign can have disastrous consequences.

Through examples in sentiment analysis (hotel reviews) and cybersecurity (failed login attempts), Lin demonstrates that flip-flopping data points concentrate around the decision boundary—the gray zone—where policies are ambiguous and even human experts disagree. These cases have no universally right answer; they depend on company-specific preferences and additional disambiguating information. The AI agent is not at fault; it is surfacing pre-existing ambiguity.

Lin proposes a solution rooted in active learning, refined for the LLM era. She recommends disagreement-based selection over uncertainty scores, since LLM uncertainty scores are unreliable—the model does not know what it does not know. Instead of expensive fine-tuning, she augments agents with two complementary memory types. Semantic memory encodes factual domain knowledge and business policies that sharpen decision boundaries. Episodic memory automatically identifies past similar cases and leverages their decisions as reference, requiring no additional human intervention—particularly effective for recurring false-positive alerts in cybersecurity. Cases that episodic memory cannot resolve are routed to human review, whose output is then distilled into semantic memory for future use.

This workflow yields three benefits: significantly improved consistency making the agent more trustworthy; efficient quality control where only a subset of outputs flagged by active learning need human review; and continuous adaptation to customer-specific environments. Experiments on 93 cybersecurity alerts run three times showed that without intervention, approximately a quarter flip-flopped; episodic memory resolved about 15%, leaving roughly 10% for human disambiguation.

Lin's three core takeaways: inconsistency is not usually a model problem—focus on label issues and insufficient information; model disagreement is a feature, not a bug—treat each as a learning opportunity; and fine-tuning is not the only option—semantic and episodic memory provide a lightweight path to continuous improvement.

sections.title: Speaker introduction and background
sections.summary: Diane Lin introduces herself and her journey through continual learning (PhD, Imperial College London), one-shot learning (MIT with Josh Tenenbaum), Alexa question answering, Vicarious (now Google DeepMind), Zscaler cybersecurity, and co-founding Culminate (acquired by Datadog). She now leads development of self-evolving agents at Datadog.

sections.title: The inconsistency problem
sections.summary: Lin presents the core problem: same model, same input, but semantically different outputs. She distinguishes this from mere wording variation and shows it causes trust issues—especially in cybersecurity where flip-flopping between malicious and benign verdicts undermines customer confidence.

sections.title: Root cause: the gray zone
sections.summary: Flip-flopping data points concentrate near decision boundaries where policies are ambiguous and even human experts disagree. Through hotel review and failed-login examples, Lin shows these cases depend on company-specific preferences and additional disambiguating information. The agent is surfacing pre-existing ambiguity, not failing.

sections.title: Active learning pipeline
sections.summary: Lin describes the traditional active learning cycle: train, predict, identify uncertain or disagreed data points, have humans review and label, retrain. For LLMs, she recommends disagreement-based selection over uncertainty scores (which are unreliable) and lighter-weight solutions over expensive fine-tuning.

sections.title: Semantic and episodic memory
sections.summary: Lin proposes augmenting agents with semantic memory (factual domain knowledge and business policies that sharpen decision boundaries) and episodic memory (leveraging past similar cases when reasoning has not been distilled), enabling continuous adaptation without fine-tuning.

sections.title: Episodic memory workflow and memory selection
sections.summary: Episodic memory automatically references past similar cases without waiting for human-distilled reasoning. It resolves recurring cases—especially false-positive cybersecurity alerts—as low-hanging fruit for automation. Semantic and episodic memory are complementary: episodic handles recurring situations automatically; unresolved cases go to human review, whose output is distilled into semantic memory for future use.

sections.title: Benefits of the solution
sections.summary: The solution brings three benefits: improved consistency making the agent more trustworthy; efficient quality control where only a subset flagged by active learning needs review; and continuous adaptation to customer-specific environments. Labeling effort is small but high-return.

sections.title: Experiment results
sections.summary: On 93 cybersecurity alerts run three times, approximately a quarter flip-flop without intervention. After applying episodic memory, about 15% become consistent. The remaining 10% still flip—sometimes due to no past reference, sometimes still disagreeing after second thought—and are handled by human review with additional knowledge injection.

sections.title: Takeaways and acknowledgments
sections.summary: Three takeaways: inconsistency is not usually a model problem—focus on label issues and insufficient information; model disagreement is a feature, not a bug—treat each as a learning opportunity; fine-tuning is not the only option—augment with semantic and episodic memory. Lin thanks colleagues at Datadog including Ditun, Harsh, Anusha, Stefan, Saeed, and Mati, plus the Beats Secured Analyst team.
